## Dragonfire adept

Dragonfire adepts were wielders of draconic magic and arcane power although not in the conventional sense associated with draconic sorcerers. Rather than arcane magic, or even spells, dragonfire adepts emulated draconic powers by infusing their very souls with the raw magic of dragons, allowing them to draw upon a direct link with the nature of draconic existence and channel it through invocations akin to those of warlocks.

Activities
Dragonfire adepts divided their time between practicing their dragon breath, studying arcane invocations, and working to build a strong base of friends and allies. They kept in mind the nobility and grace of the dragons they sought to understand and acted in all ways as they would expect a dragon to, thus making them fierce friends as well as terrible foes, and confident in their every action.  However, while they saw the value of treasure, they were not defined or slowed by their property, considering self-improvement the only kind worth their time, and taking every opportunity to test themselves against the challenges of the world.

However, the concerns and biases of their own people colored the perspectives of dragonfire adepts. Their desire to prove themselves draconic layered over the more typical interests, rather than becoming an all-consuming obsession. No matter what kind of person a dragonfire adept was, they were universally imposing figures. Hearty, learned and cunning, they could be be masters of war or lore with equal ease. They remained alert for new sources of draconic knowledge and investigate likely leads or promising instructors.

Dragonfire adepts could be of any alignment, often acting similar to dragons that shared their general outlook. Good adepts were bold champions of justice and freedom who brought the power of dragons to aid those in need, nobly defending the weak, frightened and downtrodden. Evil adepts were cruel tyrants and merciless raiders who imposed their wills on others, built strongholds and dominated lands, and always sought riches and power, uncaring of who was hurt in their hungry pursuit for more. Adepts of good, evil, law and chaos were about equally common, although they were frequently found among good creatures and less so among evil ones. Neutral adepts meanwhile were rare, the urge to delve into the mysteries of draconic energies coming more easily to those with strong beliefs and the will to pursue them.

Culture
Dragonfire adepts spent their lives learning the secrets of a race older and stronger than their own, studying arguably the oldest and most powerful force a mortal could manipulate, that of a dragon's breath. They were devoted to understanding and emulating the ways of dragons, an interest strong enough to motivate years of difficult study, practice and experimentation. Such focus was likely rooted in a life-changing event involving a dragon, whether their breath brought salvation or tragedy.

Yet the quest for dragon-like powers never eclipsed in importance what the adepts wanted to achieve with that power. They remained steadfast in their goals, typically something simple but grand that required years or even a lifetime of work. This could be righting an ancient wrong, founding their own school, community or kingdom, eliminating an entire group of foes, or just being acknowledged by true dragons as one of their own.

Dragonfire adepts could be found in all manner of civilizations, from primitive tribes, where they acted as mystics not dissimilar to dragon shamans, to noble families of draconic descent.

Most dragonfire adepts paid little attention to religion, focusing more on dragons than deities. Among those with religious tendencies, members of the draconic pantheon were popular choices they were willing to worship even where such faiths were rare (and could very well be the source of their powers), or they were drawn to the same gods as sorcerers. Furthermore, adepts were aware of their constant struggle to become more like another species, and revered figures in history who accomplished this to impressive degrees.

Prerequisites
The source of the power used by dragonfire adepts was sometimes similar to that of sorcerers, where they accessed the innate power of their own blood. In such cases, the adept was either descended from an extremely powerful dragon of their homeland or rediscovered a long-lost link to an ancient, powerful wyrm. Sorcerers, especially half-dragon ones, could duplicate many of the abilities of dragonfire adepts such that it could be difficult to distinguish them.

Alternatively, the power of a dragonfire adept could be acquired by forging pacts with powerful draconic beings, such as dragon deities or dragon ascendants. Dragon gods were the most common sources of such pacts, with Tiamat and Bahamut making the most. The next most common sources were powerful users of draconic magic and augmented dragons with extraplanar or otherwise unusual power. In Faerûn, such dragons include the likes of the pseudonatural dragon Arsekaslyx, the most powerful sorcerer of true dragonkind, Nexus, or the dracoliches Alasklerbanbastos or Dretchroyaster.

Abilities
Dragonfire adepts could achieve with their breath weapons effects that not even dragons themselves could match. On the lower end of their abilities, they could unleash blasts of elemental energies in lines or cones, but as they gained power they accessed the secondary breath weapons of metallic dragons and other exotic powers. At their mightiests, adepts could unleash the discorporating breath of Bahamut, which disintegrated its targets, or the fivefold breath of Tiamat, which unleashed five breath weapons at once. Yet, while their breath weapon was their most obvious draconic link, dragonfire adepts learned many powerful abilities as they grew, tapping into new powers the deeper they delved into the draconic magic in their souls.

The magic of dragonfire adepts was more primal, if not less tricky, than that of true spells, a repertoire of spell-like abilities known as "draconic invocations", which allowed them to focus the energy that suffused their souls. Invocations existed on a scale of least, lesser, greater and dark, each more powerful than the last. The invocations an adept chose to learn strongly shaped their abilities, and all invocations at an adept's disposal could be used at will, but like spells could be disrupted if their concentration faltered or they wore armor, and all of them required somatic movements.

As they gained power, dragonfire adepts gained thick and scaly skin that provided them natural protection, usually but not always of the same chromatic or metallic hue of their outlook and alignment, and would eventually start to resist magic. They would become immune to paralyzing and sleep-inducing effects just as dragons were, as well as to their unnerving presence, and more easily fraternize with draconic creatures.

Dragonfire adepts were heavily invested in combat prowess due to the confrontational nature of breath weapons, but had some versatility due to their invocations. They could be bottomless sources of arcane destruction, help provide support, confuse and weaken foes, or bring sage wisdom. They served best at hitting several foes from a middling distance, generally relying on allies to keep enemies at bay, and while they lacked the sheer offensive, defensive, or ranged abilities that others brought to the table, they had a unique resistance to magic and ability to improve the prowess and circumstances of those around them.
Relationships

The reception dragonfire adepts received from communities corresponded to how their cultures regarded dragons, and those who would emulate them. In places that suffered from draconic depredations, the people were often fearful or hostile towards anyone with their powers, regardless of their moral alignment, whereas in areas where dragons were perceived as defenders or sages, they were more likely to be seen like sorcerers, as great manipulators of magic. In any case, dragonfire adepts were often feared and misunderstood, for they carried the same aura of awesome power, mystery, and terrifying intensity found in true dragons. They were dealt with most savvily in places where they were common.

Dragonfire adepts were tolerant of all manner of peoples, professions and paths to power, so long as they were respected and had compatible personalities and outlooks. They valued study, discipline and raw power in particularly however, and could most appreciate those who showed similar traits. They got along well with spellcasters for example (bards and druids in particular), because they could see them delve into the essence of their focus (such as music or nature) just as they delved into the essence of dragonkind. They were similarly impressed by fighters and monks, who had devoted themselves to mastery of combat and self-improvement, although monks themselves were often puzzled by the adepts, seeing them as fools seeking to become something freakish at best and monstrous at worst. It was sorcerers who were strongly drawn to dragonfire adepts however, for they oft-shared a primal link to dragonkind.

Most dragonfire adepts were humans, elves, or half-elves, since the study of dragonkind was not unlike that of arcane magic. A surprising number of them were half-orcs, who sought either a place for themselves or to create one by force. It was not uncommon for dragonborn of Bahamut to become dragonfire adepts, their reawakening by Xymor granting them the innate power to manifest dragon magic and breath.

Dwarves were rarely dragonfire adepts, and in fact were extremely suspicious of them; they had an ancient enmity with dragonkind, and viewed dragonfire adepts as two-legged versions of the greedy, treasure-loving monsters that often raided their settlements. They were especially doubtful of dwarf dragonfire adepts, who they saw as traitors to their own race. Most halflings and gnomes lacked the burning drive needed to become dragonfire adepts.

History
There were a few notable figures who appeared in the legends of dragonfire adepts. One was Gannon Darkheart, a human whose ancestry had the blood of black dragons mixed in generations prior. Born into noble life, his avarice and wild temper led to him becoming an outcast, and so he sought to become more dragon-like to punish his community for their scorn. Not actively evil but unconcerned with morality, he could never be trusted to keep his word and willingly allied with anyone that could help him with his goal. He charged heedless into battle with the most destructive powers, assuming he could kill anything before it got the chance to harm him. Ultimately he earned his place beside true dragons by defeating the gold dragon Aghutyr in single combat and taking his tower, turning it into his own kingdom and turning the area around it into a dread marsh.

By contrast, Vorelei Frilltips had no initial draconic leanings. She began life poor and homeless on the streets of a large elf city, but with an innate sense of fair play and concern for those in trouble. Her bravery drew the attention of Gaulirden, a silver dragon secretly living in the city who took her under his wing and raised her with his older children, where she learned draconic ways and assumed their powers to help the less fortunate. She destroyed the Circle of Fire, a vile school for evil wizards, and ultimately gave her life defending a town from a blackguard's army long enough for the innocent to escape. A council of good dragons buried her as one of their own, the honor she never asked for in life granted to her in death.

It is unclear if these stories are legends from the ancient past, brought over from other the dragonfire adepts of other worlds, or fictional altogether, allegories used by dragonfire adepts to explore their philosophies and beliefs.

Notable members
 Nevelaster Rellicraun, one of the foulest dragonfire adepts in Faerûn. Allegedly descended from a human and an abishai, the Untheric tiefling was both an infernal warlock and dragonfire adept. Some Tiamatan clerics in Unther believe he was vital in the goddesses' plans to take over the Realms.

 The Light of Xymor, a group of five reclusive, Dragonborn of Bahamut dragonfire adepts who went on a mission in the Underdark beneath Vaasa, possibly to stage an attack against an insidious group of Tiamatan clerics known as the Handmaidens of the Undying Queen.

## Dragon knight

Dragon knight was a rare epic spell that allowed for the summoning of an adult red dragon at a location chosen by the spell caster.

Effects
As of the Year of Wild Magic, 1372 DR, casting the spell led to the summoning of an adult chaotic evil red dragon. The dragon had to be summoned within 8 meters (26 feet) of the caster. The dragon fought alongside the caster.

The presence of the dragon lasted around two minutes, after which it vanished. The spell could not be countered, interrupted, or dispelled using normal spells. To prevent the spell from being cast, one had to, for example, use an epic version of counterspell.

Development
Before it could be cast, dragon knight had to be developed. Both divine and arcane casters could develop this spell. Developing an epic spell was different from learning normal spells. Once an epic spell was developed, the caster knew the spell. A developed epic spell became a part of the caster and could even be prepared without a spellbook (if a wizard was the caster). Only those well-versed in spellcraft could develop dragon knight.

Components
The spell required verbal and somatic components.

## Dreamwraith

Dreamwraiths were creatures that constantly searched for dreaming minds, hoping to take shape within them and plague the dreamers until they died.

Description
Dreamwraiths looked like humans who had torn away all trappings of humanity to reveal a twisted nightmare beneath. Walking, moving, and even acting like humans, their eyes however were wild and violent, with hands curled like claws and voices harsh and otherworldly.

Abilities
They spoke any language understood by their 'host.' They could infect their host either through natural bad luck as adventurers stumbled upon them, or as part of the mindspin spell, where a dreamwraith could be summoned to attack the victim of the spell.

Combat
The dreamwraiths were subtle killers, attacking their primary victims with despair. They would often take the form of those whom the dreamer trusted or were otherwise emotionally close to and then strike at the dreamer or their allies in the dreamscape. As any harm the dreamwraiths inflicted inside the dreamscape was not real, they would attempt to make the experience as terrible and vivid for the dreamer as they could to force the dreamer into madness. As long as the dreamer believed the harm from the dreamwraith to be real, it would seem to take effect like normal injuries, and if death was the outcome of the harm dealt, the dreamer would slip into unconsciousness until the haunting by the dreamwalker ended or allies of the dreamer managed to heal them inside the dreamscape.

History
In the, a group of adventurers returned to Ravens Bluff from the Domains of Dread where they had been for five years, but unbeknownst to them they had brought back a dreamwraith that had infiltrated the mind of one of them. Several of the adventurers died, until Emeline Carpenter, a bard of Ravens Bluff and survivor of the Domains of Dread, lay dying, ravaged by the dreamwraith. She prayed to Oghma for salvation, and an animated dragon figurine led another group of adventurers into her dreamscape to save Emeline and slay the dreamwraith.

## Dragons of the Dragon Coast

Dragons of the Dragon Coast was a history book that offered a theory for the naming origin of the Dragon Coast and recorded history of the region's dragons through the centuries, published sometimt in or before the late 14 century DR.

Contents
The work stated that numerous theories existed on the origins of the term "Dragon Coast." The topic was quite contentious, with many passionate supporters of one theory over the others. Despite all the disagreements, all admitted that the name was an apt one, as the Dragon Coast was populated by the highest number of these massive flying beasts, and the region's history recorded many notable wyrms who shaped its past.

Most sages considered the dragon named Kisonraathiisar to be one of the most prominent wyrms of history. He was slain by Saldrinar of the Seven Spells in -349 DR. But even that part of the region's history was obfuscated by legends. Some believed that Kisonraathiisar was trapped within an enchanted scepter so that the wielder could conjure Kisonraathiisar's spells at will. In turn, Saldrinar made history by founding the city of Westgate atop his lair and ruling it as the first king. Some historians claimed that the Purple Dragon of Cormyr was the Dragon Coast's inspiration, while others attributed the name to Kuldrak the Many-Taloned, a gargantuan red dragon who laired in the very southern mountains of the Thunder Peaks, long before Thauglor the Purple Dragon hatched. Kuldrak was killed by Rauthstokh "Redbones", a parent of the god-dragon Tchazzar. However, there were other candidates – Arauvrim, a small but vicious fang dragon who preyed on sailors and fishers out at sea, terrorizing for ten bloody years until he was petrified by a powerful shipborne mage and plunged to the bottom of Dragonmere. Another possible candidate was Larithylar, perhaps the most terrifying monster of all. She was known to possess bodies of creatures, including, possibly, possessing one of the dragons listed above, and still being alive as of the late 14 century DR. Larithylar, also known as "the Chameleon Dragon," was a lamia sorceress who learned magical ways of inhabiting human, humanoid, and draconic forms, and even learned to posess and controll powerful true dragon. Larithylar faked her own death centuries before the  and, by some accounts, still inhabited Westgate, seeking powerful magical items for some nefarious plot.

History
In 1374 DR, a copy of Dragons of the Dragon Coast could be found in one of the rental rooms of the Bent Mermaid Inn in the city of Westgate.

## Drone

Drone was a variety of enchanted morning stars created on the Sword Coast North in the late 14 century DR, with the original and the most powerful variety once being wielded the deaf weapon master Vondin Clatch.

Powers
There existed three variants of the Drone, each possessed a +1, +4, and +8 enchantments what made the bludgeons deadlier and guided the wielder's hand towards the target. All three versions were ensorcelled to dead sonic damage to the targets while the stronger varieties also could slow the opponents down for twelve seconds.

A Drone Morning Star could be created from an enchanted morningstar and a vial full of fairy dust.

History
The first Drone was wielded by the deaf weapon master Vondin Clatch sometime before the late 15 century DR. The master learned to use his infirmity to his advantage in battle and used Drone – a magic weapon that glowed and vibrated, dealing sonic damage to the entire area around Vondin. When his apprentice inherited the weapon, he paid a wizard to focus the weapon's destructive magics so the sonic damage only affected the target, making the weapon usable to non-deaf individuals.

More common versions of the Drone morningstars with a simpler +1 enchantment were forged by Master Blacksmith Marrok of Shining Knight Arms and Armor shop of Neverwinter to help the heroes who sought the cure from the dreaded Wailing Death of the . Later the same year, more powerful versions were created by Master Blacksmith Barun of Beorunna's Well to help the forces of Neverwinter stand against Lady Aribeth the Betrayer, who led a marching army of Luskan in the deadly but short-lived Neverwinter-Luskan war.

## Drachma

A drachma  was a type of silver coin foreign to Toril, originating from a collection of city-states on another world that were known for their daring philosophies. Among those people it was commonly abbreviated as DR.

Description
Drachmae were made from silver and weighed .

Value
While valued at an equivalent exchange to other silver coins, among the city-states they originated from drachmae, filled the role of a gold piece in terms of value.

History
In the, a small-time thief in Dhaztanar by the name of Anton Tikizaras attempted to con a group of adventurers by playing on their sympathies. He fabricated a story about a brother-in-law, saying he was supposed to deliver a cartload of silk rugs to a merchant named "Faroud" (a common name in Dhaztanar) in the city's Madinat quarter, but the brother instead robbed Anton blind and sailed away with the silk, heading west to the country of Murghom. Eventually the players agreed to pose as his distant cousins and accompany him to the silk merchant, secretly one of his compatriots.

They met in a dingy little shop, off a small alley in the heart of Madinat. There Anton assured "Faroud", a smuggler, that the foreigners would be willing to buy his stock of smuggled in wine in order to pay off his debts. He haggled the price for a bit for show, then put down a bag of drachmas as a down payment, signaling to one of his other criminal companions to leave the room.

Sometime around the late 14 century DR, a Zhentarim splinter-group called the Flight of Arrows traveled to the city of Ravens Bluff to seek asylum. Among their number was Jeridal, an experienced young lady, who alongside her allies escaped from the inn they were being kept in at Crow's End with a cone of silence so she could spend some drachmas at the local marketplace.

Appendix
Background
It is purely speculatory as to whether or not the cited instances of drachmas on Toril are truly coins from another world, namely Earth or some other Grecian inspired world, brought to Toril through one of its many portals. It is quite possible that the authors of these sources were treating the word "drachma" as a synonym for "silver coin", however, this would be a decidedly nonstandard usage of the term.

In the case of the one instance in the Land of Fate boxed set, it could be a misguided reference to dirhams. This was a Medieval Islamic coinage, whose name is a derivation of "drachma", and was also used as the name for silver Zakharan-minted coins in the book Arabian Adventures.

## Drow slave collar

Drow slave collars were a kind of magical control device used by the drow of Sschindylryn in the 15 century DR, finding extensive use during the invasion of Eveningstar.

Description

The collars were heavy metal constructions that fitted around the neck, requiring either the correct key or deft skill to remove safely.

Powers

When worn by a slave, their body was put under the control of nearby taskmasters, without their mind being directly affected. This left them lucid and aware of what was happening, without any ability to do more than speak on their own volition. Without the presence of a nearby controller they might be left to their own devices, or just left helpless as their body waited for commands.

If the collar was tampered with, such as in an escape attempt, a failsafe would instantly kill the wearer, though it could potentially be safely unlocked with proficient skills and a good dose of luck.

History

The drow of Sschindylryn used these collars on their own drow underclass, and as the war with Cormyr began they began to use them upon captured surfacer prisoners, including villagers, War Wizards, and Purple Dragons. While all groups used them, they were most common with House Avithoul, the preeminent slave traders in the city, and House Cay'Vorym, who used the slaves as entertainment in the Underdark Arena and Cay'Vorym Fighting Pit. During the war, the Sschindylrynyr used enslaved surfacers as forced labor in their various projects, but most notably expended them on the battlefield as shock troops and bodyguards, parallel to House Szind's use of reanimated Cormyreans as zombies. While the civilians were none too effective in combat, the use of unwilling Cormyreans against their own folk—often while crying for mercy or screaming in horror—was a potent psychological weapon. The only way to counter this tactic was to somehow avoid killing the collared fighters while searching for their slavemaster, who was usually hidden nearby, and then attempt to safely remove the collars without killing the victims.

Mirini Elemys was a rare example of a successful escapee. Through patience, cunning, and opportunity, she managed to unlock her own collar and escaped from the Underdark to the World Above, where she organized a devastating raid on House Avithoul's estate.

## Dreak

Dreak was a half-orc who was former slave turned pirate and the first mate of the infamous Scimitar of Fire, which was active on the Sea of Swords in the mid-to-late 14 century DR.

Relationships
He served as first mate of Captain Raurivyl Ornshield. They made an effective pair, with Dreak having the brawn and Raurivyl the brains and plans.

History
Dreak began as a slave in Amn, working on a plantation lying east of Lake Esmel that was owned by the Colwyvv family. There, he befriended a fellow slave, a human named Raurivyl.

Then, with the advent of the First Dragonspear War in the, the number of guards at the plantation were reduced. Seizing the advantage, Raurivyl, Dreak, and other slaves made their escape. However, instead of running to safe havens in the north or south, Raurivyl and Dreak went west, taking a ship and fighting a vengeful war against Amn, its merchant houses, and the Council of Six. Helming the Scimitar of Fire, they became infamous as pirates, feared by both Amnian and Calishite ship captains for over a decade by 1370 DR.

Seeking a desert island he might use as a safe haven and base, Raurivyl and Dreak took the Scimitar of Fire westward on several voyages beyond the Gull Rocks. However, they found naught but a vast expanse of empty ocean. On three occasions they encountered the naval vessels of Evermeet, which rose out of the sea, hovered in the air, and tilted to direct their strange weaponry at the Scimitar. Via magical speaking horns, the elves ordered the pirates to leave. Sensibly, Captain Ornshield obeyed, but still the flying elven ships followed them until they were long gone.

Following months of such futile searching, Raurivyl and Dreak returned to the Nelanther Isles. They sheltered the Scimitar in a cavern harbor on the island of Carcathen and later located a safehouse he wasn't yet sure about in Ilyaport in Lantan.

As of 1370 DR, after laying low for a number of months at Carcathen, Dreak, Raurivyl, and the crew had grown restless. Fortunately, the turmoil they found in Amn at the time attracted their attention. Yet they attracted another's attention too: the Rundeen mercantile organization, who desired the Scimitar of Fire's services as pirates in the Shining Sea. In trade, they offered safe havens, ship repairs, and whatever else they might wish for. However, although intrigued by a profitable alliance, Raurivyl knew the Rundeen acted much the same as their Amnian enemies and so he was just as likely, if not more so, to start targeting Rundeen shipping instead.

Despite this, the Scimitar of Fire was reported to be Rundeen pirate vessel later that year.

Draconic rings of the shore were powerful enchanted rings crafted for the survivors of the battle on the shores of the isle of Tuern in the late 15 century DR.

Powers
These pieces of magical jewelry were imbued with various enchantments that boosted the wearer's vitality, physical power, ability to deal devastating damage with lucky and precise strikes, and improved their ability to pierce enemy armor. When a draconic ring of the shore was worn together with a burning necklace of the shore and a barbaric ring of the shore, all three items boosted each other's enchantments, granting the wearer a bigger boost to their physical power, as well and enhanced their physical defense and speed of movement.

History
These items were created as a reward for the defenders and adventurers of Neverwinter, who risked their lives in a battle that took place in the 1480s DR. The Cult of the Dragon on the isle of Tuern was met with Lords' Alliance forces as well as volunteer adventurers. The survivors were rewarded with burning necklaces, draconic rings, and barbaric rings.

## Dragon loyalist's visage

Dragon loyalist's visage was a unique artifact mask, both magnificent and regal in its design, created sometime before the late 15 century DR.

Powers
The mask gave its wearer certain gravitas that commanded the attention and respect of all dragonkin. It greatly increased the wearer's physical strength and defenses in battle, as well as greatly boosted their vitality. When its wearer commanded a dragon or dragonkin mount, companion, summoned creature, or an ally, the mask granted the wearer additional boons that depended on the type of the commanded creature.

History
By the 1480s DR, the Cult of the Dragon posessed the dragon loyalist's visage. The Cult's leaders, who helmed a skirmish on the shores of the isle of Tuern, brought the artifact into battle against the defenders, heroes, and adventurers and the Lords' Alliance forces. When the Cult's men were defeated, the mask was retrieved by the forces of Neverwinter.
